rrp_conversation.content: I've completed a full scan of the current deployment. The architecture has been scaffolded with all 6 modular documentation files in docs/agents/, the canonical data store at rack/ with all subracks initialized, the .rsis/ compatibility symlink in place, and the root AGENTS.md converted to a master routing index. However, this is a shell — there is no operational runtime codebase. No evaluator, no codegen engine, no state machine, no test suite, no recovery manager. The rack/ subracks (L1-L6) are empty of telemetry. The knowledge graph has 800 raw nodes but only 7 consolidated — a utility density of 0.875%, well below the 10% threshold that would trigger concern, but still indicating the KG is essentially unused. The two critical metric gaps from the baseline are signal_coverage at 1.2/100 — meaning the system is nearly blind to incoming file changes — and insight_utilization at 0.0/100, meaning the KG is never queried during decision-making.

I verify the platform assessment. The scaffold is structurally coherent — all 6 modules, rack subracks, and symlinks are correctly placed and cross-reference cleanly. I note two implicit constraints the Domain Expert did not explicitly state but which are active: (1) the '388 tests must pass' invariant cannot yet be satisfied because no test suite exists, which creates a bootstrap paradox — we need code to write tests, but tests must exist before code is accepted. This requires a sequenced exception for the initial build phase. (2) The signal_coverage gap is not merely a metric — it's a structural absence. There is no file-watcher or signal-detection mechanism at all. Closing it to even a functional minimum (say 30/100) requires building a file-monitoring primitive. I also flag that the KG consolidation algorithm is unspecified — the ratio of 7 consolidated out of 800 raw suggests either extremely aggressive filtering or a broken pipeline. Clarity needed before we can meaningfully grow KG utility.

Acknowledged on the bootstrap paradox. I formally define 5 architectural goals for this lifecycle, ordered by dependency: Goal 1 — Establish the evaluator runtime by creating evaluator/evaluator.py with a 4-phase reasoning report structure and an EvaluatorClient stub that operates in mode='local'. This is the foundation because every L2 cycle requires an evaluation pass before patch application. Goal 2 — Build the codegen engine with a Jinja2 template environment, a fix_stub.j2 template restricted to AST-targeted diffs, and an AST coordinate parser that locates stub patterns (pass, ..., raise NotImplementedError) before patch generation. Goal 3 — Implement the lifecycle state machine as state_machine.py with the 5 states (PROPOSED, QUEUED, EXECUTING, COMPLETED, ARCHIVED), 3-attempt retry limits, and priority queue eviction logic. Goal 4 — Create an initial test suite under tests/ using pytest, starting with unit tests for the evaluator and state machine, sufficient to unblock the test absolutism invariant. Goal 5 — Build a RecoveryManager that executes git checkout to the last verified commit upon any test failure, and implement a basic KG consolidation routine that can raise utility density above 10%.

I break down each goal and score its value alignment. Goal 1 (evaluator runtime): directly aligns with robustness (structured error handling in the evaluation pass) and autonomy (removes dependency on external evaluation APIs). However, the 4-phase schema requires the agent to manually produce evaluation reports for every cycle — this creates a documentation tax that must be tracked. Goal 2 (codegen engine): aligns with maintainability (clean AST-targeted diffs) and efficiency (Jinja2 template reuse). The anti-bloat constraint from the Guardian Protocol is core here — fix_stub.j2 must be verified to never wrap a full file. I recommend adding an AST pre-validation step before template rendering. Goal 3 (state machine): aligns with coherence (structured state transitions) and stability (retry limits and eviction prevent infinite loops). The state machine should log every transition to rack/L2/ for traceability. Goal 4 (test suite): aligns with robustness and stability — this is the gate that enforces test absolutism. I recommend starting with a minimal set (~10 tests) that cover the evaluator and state machine, then expanding. Goal 5 (RecoveryManager + KG): aligns with stability and identity. The RecoveryManager is essential for rollback safety; the KG consolidation routine needs a documented algorithm. Without it, the utility density will remain stagnant regardless of node count.

I formalize the explicit constraint bounds for this lifecycle. Zero-Deletion Directive: rack/ and .rsis/ are immutable — no rm -rf or global cleanup may touch them under any circumstances. Anti-Bloat: every codegen output must pass an AST diff validation - if the patch wraps more than the targeted function body, the generation must be rejected and re-rendered. Test Absolutism: the initial test suite must reach at least 10 passing tests before any non-test code change can be accepted, scaling toward 388. Manual Oracle: every L2 cycle must produce a 4-phase evaluation report (goal_analysis, constraint_extraction, ambiguity_assessment, evaluation) logged to the pulse sequence. Documentation Parity: every file creation or modification must include a corresponding update to CHANGELOG.md and, if applicable, the relevant module doc in docs/agents/. Version Discipline: patch bumps (0.0.Z) are automatic on successful verified cycles; minor bumps (0.Y.0) require user confirmation; major (X.0.0) requires full development sign-off. I also add a new lifecycle-specific constraint: Bootstrap Sequencing — during the initial build phase only, the test absolutism invariant is relaxed to 'minimum 10 passing tests' until the test suite organically grows to full coverage.

I accept the constraint formalization and the bootstrap sequencing exception — it resolves the bootstrap paradox cleanly. However, I flag 4 remaining ambiguities. Ambiguity 1 — KG Consolidation Threshold: the Domain Expert states 'utility density above 10%' as a goal, but the algorithm for consolidation is undefined. Is it based on access frequency? Semantic similarity? Manual curation tags? Without a documented algorithm, the metric cannot be reliably moved. Ambiguity 2 — Signal Coverage Implementation: closing signal_coverage from 1.2 to a functional level requires a file-monitoring mechanism (inotify, polling, or git-aware diff detection). The architecture does not specify which approach is preferred. A polling-based watcher is simplest but incurs latency; inotify is efficient but platform-dependent. Ambiguity 3 — Priority Queue Eviction Policy: the state machine spec says 'lower-ranked tasks are automatically evicted' when capacity is reached, but the ranking tiebreaker is unspecified. If two tasks have equal priority rank, does the system evict the older task, the one with more failed attempts, or the one with lower value alignment weight? Ambiguity 4 — Evaluation Decision Escalation: the 4-phase evaluator produces PASS, DISMISS, or HOLD decisions. If a HOLD is issued (as it is now in pulse-001), what is the escalation path? Does the system wait for user input, automatically re-evaluate after changes, or escalate to an L3 self-direction loop? The current architecture does not define the HOLD timeout or retry behavior.

I resolve each ambiguity in turn. Ambiguity 1 — KG Consolidation: the algorithm is frequency-weighted semantic similarity. Nodes are scored by (access_count * 0.6) + (semantic_overlap_score * 0.4). Pairs with combined similarity above 0.75 are merged. This will be documented in the consolidation module docstring. Ambiguity 2 — Signal Coverage: we start with a lightweight polling watcher using os.stat() mtime checks on a configured watch list, operating at 30-second intervals. This avoids platform dependencies and is sufficient to move the metric from 1.2 to at least 30. An inotify backend can be added as an L4 optimization later. Ambiguity 3 — Priority Queue Tiebreaker: eviction favors retaining tasks with higher value alignment weight (sum of reinforced_counts of aligned axioms). If still tied, evict the older task (lower creation timestamp). This ensures value-reinforced work is deprioritized last. Ambiguity 4 — HOLD Escalation: a HOLD decision suspends the cycle and writes the evaluation report to pulses/latest.json. The system then waits for explicit user input — either a directive to proceed, modify, or cancel. No automatic re-evaluation or L3 escalation occurs during HOLD. This preserves the manual oracle's authority over lifecycle decisions.

All 4 ambiguities resolved with concrete, implementable specifications. I synthesize the baseline directional strategy. This lifecycle (Lifecycle 1) proceeds in two phases. Phase A — Scaffold Runtime: execute priority queue tasks 1 through 5 in ranked order, each verified by a manual 4-phase evaluation. Phase B — First L2 Cycle: once the evaluator, codegen, state machine, test suite, and recovery manager exist, execute a single end-to-end L2 pass on a real target stub to validate the full pipeline. Success criteria for Phase A: evaluator/evaluator.py outputs valid 4-phase reports, codegen engine renders AST-targeted diffs only, state machine transitions through all 5 states, minimum 10 pytest tests pass, RecoveryManager performs a verified git checkout rollback on a deliberately failed test. Success criteria for Phase B: a real stub is detected, patched via AST-targeted codegen, evaluated with a PASS decision, git-applied, and all tests pass. I log the final priority queue with resolved weights. Confidence in this alignment: 0.90.
